results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

results.draft_locus: Introduction ¶4
results.quote: then how the pieces fit together with a PIM and what channels document
results.finding: The intro reader predicted the sections and their order correctly, but not the expected evidence: it read the Google and marketplace rules as passing examples, said the introduction 'does not say whether specific documentation will be quoted or cited' and that it 'promises no ... external case studies beyond the fictional company'; it did not foresee platform and channel documentation or standards (GS1, schema.org) as evidence, and found 'what channels document' vague. The introduction never signals that the chapter rests on platform, channel and standards documentation.
Every outliner summary matches the controlling idea of its aligned spec paragraph in the same order (callouts unmatched by design); structure check also passes.

results.draft_locus: In Practice ¶5
results.quote: The PIM is also the first prerequisite of **W8**, readiness for the AI agents named among the consumers above
results.finding: The outliner found two ideas: the consumer-by-consumer migration with its reconciliation, and the PIM as the prerequisite for AI-agent readiness (W8). The spec's own controlling idea for p48 bundles both, so the draft follows the spec.

Every unit ties to a supporting claim: scene and ownership to S2, product model and identifiers to S1, channel documentation and rule 3 to S3, choices/trade-offs/stages to S4, failures to S5; context paragraphs (p03, p19, p35) frame S1/S2/S4.

Each table (identity, ownership, trade-offs, stages, flows), figure (1-4, each with an explanatory caption) and quotation (Shopify, schema.org, GS1, commercetools, Akeneo/Pimcore, Microsoft, Google, bol) is framed or followed by a sentence saying what it shows (e.g. 'Two things stand out', 'The setting carries out the ownership decision; it cannot make it', 'none gives a testable threshold').

results.draft_locus: Across Scale Stages: When It Fits and When It Limits ¶1
results.quote: Which arrangement fits changes as a merchant grows through the book's four stages
results.finding: Declared relationship is time, carrying over 'the recommendation and its conditions'. The opening does not pick up the recommendation; it arrives straight after 'The count of producers and consumers decides, not revenue or the stage', so the stage-and-revenue table reads as contradicting it rather than extending it over time (both flow readers stopped here).

All other boundaries express the declared relationship and pick up the declared known information (e.g. 'Where we are in the order's journey', 'Read against this table', 'Kestrel & Pine's content row needs an owner', 'Once the test says a PIM is needed', 'Even with an owner in place', 'With the product described once and owned per attribute').

results.draft_locus: How the Pieces Fit Together With a PIM ¶2
results.quote: (master data management and product lifecycle management, the systems where products are designed)
results.finding: MDM and PLM are on does_not_know; the gloss is given but reads as if both are 'the systems where products are designed', which fits PLM only (flow reader A, item 9).

results.draft_locus: How the Pieces Fit Together With a PIM ¶6
results.quote: makes its first two enrichment levels (sets of attributes it asks for) mandatory
results.finding: 'Enrichment' was defined at the fourth choice as the PIM's activity; here it is reused as bol's term for something else, and the gloss is easy to miss (flow reader B, item 12).

Every other does_not_know term (option, option value, SKU vs GTIN, EAN-13, GTIN-14, GS1, attribute, attribute set, taxonomy, mapping, bundle, configurable product, digital good, lifecycle, enrichment, syndication, feed, structured data, schema.org, staged and published data, CE marking) is glossed at or before first use; terms from Part I are used as known.

results.draft_locus: Introduction ¶3
results.quote: The price, discount and stock in the next chapters are all looked up by the SKU and the GTIN, so the codes come first.
results.finding: Two reasons for the chapter's place (content changes most slowly; codes are the keys) sit in consecutive sentences and the 'so' leaves readers unsure which one it rests on; the step to 'the codes come first' in a chapter mostly about content ownership made both readers re-read.

results.draft_locus: What a Product Is: Four Things That Share a Name ¶5
results.quote: Other product shapes, and other platforms' names for the grid, keep the identifier rule. In each, every sellable item keeps its own identity:
results.finding: The lead-in promises that each bullet is about identity, but the digital-good and gift-card bullets are about fulfillment, tax and finance, and the configurable product is another name for the grid, not another shape; both readers re-read to work out what the list was for.

results.draft_locus: What a Product Is: Four Things That Share a Name ¶6
results.quote: **Variant limits shape catalogs.** A shop platform may cap how many size, color and other combinations one product can hold
results.finding: The text leaves the variant grid for the list of other product shapes and then returns to the grid with variant limits; reader B wants this paragraph right after the option/variant paragraph, and reader A wants the configurable-product (grid) point moved next to it, the same split of grid material. The spec orders p14 before p09a.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader A, section 4 (fourth reordering bullet)

results.draft_locus: What a Product Is: Four Things That Share a Name ¶7
results.quote: The grid and its identifiers should neither change nor be split; the fields around them do.
results.finding: 'do' is ambiguous after 'neither change nor be split' (change, or be split?); both readers paused to resolve it.

results.draft_locus: What a Product Is: Four Things That Share a Name ¶9
results.quote: Kestrel & Pine sells in three countries and two languages in Belgium alone, so every description exists at least three times by design
results.finding: The countries and languages are not named, so the reader must work out three countries, two Belgian languages and therefore three languages to reach 'three times'; both readers re-read.

results.draft_locus: Trade-offs ¶2
results.quote: The count of producers and consumers decides, not revenue or the stage.
results.finding: The very next section is a table organised by stage and revenue band, and nothing reconciles 'the stage does not decide' with it; both readers wondered why the stage view follows a sentence discounting stages (reader A also notes the roadmap sets the test after the stage view). The spec places trade-offs before stages; the draft could reconcile with one sentence, so fault is unclear.

results.draft_locus: How the Pieces Fit Together With a PIM ¶1
results.quote: A **PIM**, the scene's shared place for product content, is the editorial system where product data is created, enriched, translated and approved before it is syndicated to channels.
results.finding: A third definition of PIM (after the opener and the scene), plus a re-definition of feed, arrives after the term has been used for the whole chapter and reads as out of place; both readers suggest moving it into option 4 or dropping it. The spec's p21 prescribes this definition here.

results.draft_locus: How the Pieces Fit Together With a PIM ¶9
results.quote: commercetools builds the same idea into its product model with staged and current data
results.finding: Earlier the same commercetools split was called staged versus published data; the change of word made both readers check whether this was a different idea.

results.draft_locus: In Practice ¶2
results.quote: building on March's table of one owner per kind of record ([[boundaries-and-systems-of-record]])
results.finding: 'March's table' has not been mentioned in this chapter; both readers had to guess it comes from another chapter.

results.draft_locus: When It Goes Wrong ¶6
results.quote: for two days bol received stale data (stock figures in that case; a content sync fails the same way)
results.finding: The worked example of a product-content failure is a stock incident, in a chapter that has just said stock travels on a separate path; the parenthesis admits it but both readers found it borrowed or off-topic. The spec prescribes this case.

results.draft_locus: Introduction ¶4
results.quote: Four ways to arrange product data follow, with their trade-offs by scale stage and the test for when a PIM is needed
results.finding: The roadmap merges trade-offs and stages and puts the test after the stage view, while the body gives the test in Trade-offs before the separate stage section (flow reader A, item 2).

results.draft_locus: The Choices ¶3
results.quote: the content ends up in spreadsheets beside the ERP, which is Kestrel & Pine's situation
results.finding: In the scene Kestrel & Pine's descriptions live in the shop platform, with costs in the ERP and translations in spreadsheets, a mix of options 1-3; calling it option 2's situation does not match the scene (flow reader A, item 6). The spec's p32 evidence sets this up.

results.draft_locus: In Practice ¶6
results.quote: The numbers that matter are small.
results.finding: Sets up numbers the paragraph does not deliver: what follows is mostly qualitative (flow reader A, item 13). The spec says 'results', not 'numbers'.

results.draft_locus: Setting the Scene at Kestrel & Pine: The Season That Was Typed Four Times ¶4
results.quote: Waypoint, Kestrel & Pine's improvement program, addresses this in decision W3: introduce a PIM in Q3 2027 for content and attributes.
results.finding: The answer (buy a PIM) is given before the product model, ownership and the PIM test, so the later test reads as an after-the-fact justification rather than a check the reader applies (flow reader B, item 2). The spec places W3 here.

results.draft_locus: Who Owns Which Field: Producers, Consumers and the System of Record ¶4
results.quote: the spreadsheets because the product team works there; the ERP a name because an item must have one
results.finding: Elided verbs make the clauses read briefly as fragments; followable but slow (flow reader B, item 7).

results.draft_locus: Trade-offs ¶2
results.quote: Kestrel & Pine crossed the line around 2021–2022, when it added marketplaces (2021) and a third country (2022) to a Belgian storefront that already ran in two languages.
results.finding: 'A Belgian storefront' clashes with Dutch as the home language elsewhere, and the text never says why a need dated 2021-2022 leads to a PIM only in Q3 2027 (flow reader B, item 8).

results.draft_locus: What to Take Away ¶1
results.quote: A scheduled comparison finds those failures after they happen; ownership prevents them.
results.finding: Contradicts the failure section's opening 'Even with an owner in place, product data fails quietly': those failures were presented as ones that occur with ownership, and the takeaway now says ownership prevents them; reader B stopped here (flow reader B, item 15).

The introduction opens on a concrete case (the Ridgewalker's 24 variants and a correction that reaches one channel), states a claim and places the chapter; none of placeholder, restated question, dictionary, dawn of man or book report.

The conclusion does not open with 'in conclusion', does not merely restate the thesis, introduces no new subtopic and holds no body evidence; it sorts points by how settled they are and ends with application questions and a hand-off.

p57 joins identifiers, per-attribute owner and the route back into one design that no single section states, and p60 says why it matters: a PIM bought without the ownership table 'becomes a fifth copy with a login'.
p57 returns explicitly to the corrected waterproof rating that reached the web shop and not the marketplace, and names what was missing.
Reader answers 'no, it should not buy', states the more-than-one-producer and more-than-one-consumer test, says revenue does not decide, and names the Giant's Boots: matches expected.

Reader names the missing single owning system per attribute with a one-way path, places the correction in the owning system (PIM, or the declared shop platform at small scale), and quotes the read-only editor rule: matches expected.
Reader says retire and reissue, map the old one for history, never edit in place or reuse, because orders, warehouses and marketplaces are keyed on SKU and GTIN: matches expected.
